skills.name: deck-storyline
skills.description: Turning a brief into a deck's storyline: audience, arc, one message per slide.
skills.body:
Before any slide, decide what the audience should think or do afterwards: that is the deck's one-sentence point.

Then the arc. Pick the one that fits:
- Situation → complication → resolution (decisions, proposals).
- Why now → what → how → what we need (pitches, plans).
- Headline → evidence → implications (reviews, research).

Rules for the outline:
- One message per slide. Write each slide's title as the message itself, a full sentence ("Churn halved after onboarding changed"), not a topic ("Churn").
- Under each title, the evidence: 1–3 points, a number, or the chart that proves it. Say which visual each slide needs (chart of what, diagram of what, a big number, a quote).
- Length: about one slide per minute of talk; 8–14 slides for most briefs. Title, an agenda only when there are 4+ sections, section dividers only for long decks, a closing slide with the ask or the summary.
- Cut anything that doesn't serve the point. Put detail in an appendix, not the main flow.
Write the outline as Markdown: a numbered list of slide titles, each with its layout and its content in a few lines.

skills.name: deck-design
skills.description: Design rules for professional slides: grid, type, spacing, colour, one idea per slide.
skills.body:
- Space is the main tool. Margins stay as the base CSS sets them (88px sides, 72px top). Nothing touches an edge except full-bleed images.
- One idea per slide; at most 3–5 points, each at most two lines. If it doesn't fit at 26px, it is two slides or an appendix.
- Type: the theme's display face for titles, body face for text; never below 18px (captions), body 24–28px. Titles state the message.
- Colour: the theme's accent marks the one thing to look at (the key bar, the number, the takeaway). Everything else is ink and muted.
- Alignment: left-align text; align elements to shared edges; consistent positions for titles slide to slide.
- Data: every chart answers the slide's title. Remove gridlines, borders, legends you can replace with direct labels; label the key value; sort bars; start bars at zero.
- Vary layouts (title, points, two columns, big number, chart, quote, section) so the deck has rhythm, but repeat each layout the same way.
- No clip art, no stock-photo clichés, no gradients unless the theme has them, no drop shadows, no centred paragraphs of text.

skills.name: deck-html
skills.description: How to write a deck as HTML: the markup, layouts and base CSS, and printing it to PDF.

skills.name: deck-visuals
skills.description: Charts, diagrams and icons for slides, drawn as inline SVG.
skills.body:
Draw visuals as inline SVG with a viewBox, so they scale and print sharply.
- Bar and column charts: <rect> per value, sorted, starting at zero; label values directly on or beside bars; the key bar in var(--accent), others in var(--muted) at reduced opacity; no axis lines beyond a baseline.
- Lines: one <polyline> per series, the key one in the accent, end labels instead of a legend.
- Big numbers: a .big element with a one-line caption beats a chart with one value.
- Diagrams: boxes (<rect rx>) and arrows (<path> with a marker) on a grid; few words per box; left to right or top to bottom.
- Icons: simple line icons drawn as SVG paths (2px stroke, round caps), the same size and stroke on every slide.
- Data from carbon6: query collections and series (records_query, series_query) and chart the real numbers; say where numbers come from in a caption.
- Images: only real ones (the user's files, screenshots, product images); fit them with object-fit: cover inside a figure.

skills.name: deck-review
skills.description: Checking each rendered slide and fixing what is wrong.
skills.body:
Look at every slide's screenshot. For each, check and fix:
- Nothing overflows or is cut off; nothing touches the edges; the footer is clear of content.
- The title states the message and fits on at most two lines.
- Text is readable: no more than about 40 words of body text; no line under 18px.
- Alignment: elements share edges; spacing is even; columns line up.
- The eye goes first to what matters (the accent marks it); nothing competes with it.
- Charts: the right chart for the point, labelled, sorted, no clutter; numbers are right.
- Consistency: same layout used the same way across slides; same title position.
Fix in deck.html and screenshot again until every slide passes. Then look at the whole deck once more as a sequence: does the story flow, is there rhythm, is anything repeated?

templates.name: deck
templates.description: A deck from a brief: outline → theme → build → review → HTML and PDF.
templates.prompt:
Make a presentation deck from this brief:

{{input}}

Use the skills deck-storyline, deck-design, deck-html, deck-visuals and deck-review. Work in a folder decks/<short-name>/ under the working directory.

1. Add a record to the decks collection (title, brief, audience, stage outlining, folder).
2. Write the outline (deck-storyline). Ask the user to approve it with decision_request: the outline in the document, options "Looks good" and "Change it" (they say what in the note), group decks. Then end your turn and wait: the answer comes back as a message. Revise and ask again until they approve. Save the outline in the record.
3. Read the themes collection. Ask which theme with decision_request (one option per theme, its mood as what it does). Wait for the answer. Set the record's stage to building and its theme.
4. Build deck.html (deck-html, deck-visuals, deck-design).
5. Review: render every slide with kit_run (kit decks-render, tool slides, into <folder>/slides) and read each image. Fix what deck-review finds and look again, until every slide passes. Set the stage to reviewing while you do.
6. Print deck.pdf with kit_run (tool pdf); if the brief asks for PowerPoint, make deck.pptx too (tool pptx). Publish deck.html, deck.pdf (and deck.pptx) with publish_file.
7. Update the record: stage delivered, the files. Tell the user what you made in two lines.

memory.text: This realm makes presentation decks. Every deck is HTML first (deck.html), checked slide by slide as images from the decks-render kit, and delivered as HTML and PDF (and PowerPoint when asked).
